knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=T)
if(!require(nlme)) {install.packages("nlme")}
```


# 1. Data preparation 

The longitudinal data are from an experiment to study the effect of intermittent fasting on the weights of 15 participants, each measured weekly during the intervention.

\scriptsize
```{r desc, warning=F}
df <- dat <- read.csv("~/Documents/IF/dataset/IFStudy-Weights_DATA_2023-05-25_0957.csv")
str(df)
```
\normalsize
``````{r desc.contd, warning=F}
dat$sunday_weight <- as.numeric(dat$sunday_weight)
dat <- na.omit(dat) #exclude rows that have missing values (blank, "N/A", NA) in any column
dat <- dat[,c(1,5,6)]
colnames(dat) <- c("ID", "Week", "Weight")
dat$ID <- factor(dat$ID)
table(dat$ID) #number of observations for each subject
dat <- droplevels(subset(dat, !(ID %in% c("IF-007","IF-014")))) #exclude insufficient data
dat$Week <- dat$Week - 1 #start from Week 0
str(dat)
```


\newpage
# 2. Modeling

In a linear mixed-effects regression, each subject has its intercept and slope (i.e., random intercepts and random slopes).

```{r nlme}
fit <- nlme::lme(fixed=Weight ~ Week, 
                 random=~Week | ID,      #random intercept and slope for each subject
                 data=dat, method="ML")
summary(fit)
```

The $p$-value of .0013 for the random slopes is statistically significant at an alpha level of .01 ($t=-3.257988$, $\textit{df}=213$). Hence, reject the null hypothesis that the `Week` effect is zero.

```{r coef}
# -0.38742 + c(-1,1)* 1.96 * 0.118913
nlme::intervals(fit) #95% confidence intervals for the fixed effects
coef(fit)
```


&nbsp;
&nbsp;


# 3. Summary

A one unit increase in time (a week) is associated with an average weight **loss** of 0.39 lbs (95% confidence interval 0.15-0.62 lbs), according to a longitudinal study of 14 subjects over a minimum of 12 weeks and a maximum of 26 weeks from 2021 to 2022.

When examining the individual fit, IF-010, on the contrary, was gaining weight during the intervention.
